sections.title: Interview answer
sections.content:
A word-frequency counter tokenizes text and increments a map entry for each token. The tokenization rule decides what the program considers a word.

`strings.Fields` splits an in-memory string around runs of Unicode whitespace. A loop over the returned words updates `map[string]int` with `counts[word]++`.

For example, `go Go go` produces separate keys unless the program first applies a chosen case rule. `go, go` also keeps `go,` distinct because `Fields` does not remove punctuation.

There is no universal word definition. The application must state its language, normalization, punctuation, memory, and maximum-token requirements before choosing a tokenizer.

Use `strings.Fields` when whitespace-separated tokens are the actual requirement and the text already fits comfortably in memory. It is small, Unicode-aware for spaces, and easy to test.

sections.title: Why the failure happens: word counting in Go
sections.content:
Failures around word counting in Go usually come from one incorrect assumption about ownership, state, ordering, or lifetime. Finding that assumption is more useful than adding a defensive line at random.

Lowercasing can combine `Go` and `go`, while trimming punctuation can combine `go` and `go,`; neither choice is universally correct. A count discrepancy should be reduced to the smallest input that produces two unexpected tokens, then fixed in the tokenizer rather than patched in the map.

sections.title: The important trade-off: word counting in Go
sections.content:
word counting in Go and a manual text scanner solve related problems, but they expose different guarantees. The best choice follows from the guarantee the program actually needs.

A string helper sees the whole input at once. Scanner offers bounded incremental processing and a default word split function, while `FieldsFunc` offers custom separators for an in-memory string. A hand-written state machine is justified only when token rules cannot be expressed clearly by those tools.
